..(Friday through Wednesday)
Issued at 346 PM EDT WED SEP 2 2026

At the start of the long term period, eastern Kentucky will still
be feeling the influence of anomalously strong upper level 
ridging, although less strongly than in previous days. Meanwhile, 
troughing associated with a closed low over Quebec will sit due 
north of the forecast area, with another trough over the western 
CONUS. Throughout the day, this pattern will amplify 
significantly, with flow over the forecast area becoming 
northwesterly by the afternoon and evening hours as the eastern 
CONUS trough digs farther south and ridging retrogrades westward. 
The breakdown of this ridge over our area will allow for 
marginally cooler temperatures compared to previous days (with 
highs generally in the low 90s, barring any convective 
interference). This will also support a more active pattern 
overall. Rain chances return to the area as early as Friday 
afternoon/evening as a shortwave approaches ahead of a weak cold 
front. Isolated to scattered thunderstorms will be possible with 
this feature, particularly in the northern and eastern portions of
the forecast area where height falls will be the most robust. 
Given the hot and moist weather, storms will have ample 
instability to work with, and strong to perhaps severe 
thunderstorms are not off the table. LREF mean surface CAPE values
look to be around 2000 J/kg across the forecast area on Friday 
afternoon, with individual deterministic model soundings showing 
even stronger instability (in excess of 3000 J/kg). Shear looks to
be fairly unimpressive, with bulk shear generally in the 20-25 kt
range and hodographs generally unidirectional; however, with some
models indicating the potential for convection moving through 
eastern Kentucky very early Friday morning, it is not 
inconceivable that any lingering boundaries could serve to enhance
shear locally, although it remains much too early to pinpoint 
specifics. Given this environment, the Storm Prediction Center has
placed eastern Kentucky in a Marginal (Level 1/5) Risk for Severe
Weather, with damaging wind gusts as the primary hazard. 
Atmospheric moisture will also be rather high, with LREF mean PW 
values in the 1.5-1.7 in range (80th percentile or higher compared
to climatology). As such, torrential downpours will also be 
possible within thunderstorms.

Overnight Friday into Saturday morning, the aforementioned cold 
front will sag south through eastern Kentucky, providing another 
focus for showers and storms. There is still significant model 
disagreement regarding the timing and extent of convective 
coverage associated with this frontal passage, resulting in NBM 
PoPs likely being a bit underdone compared to true rain chances, 
although uncertainty remains too high to refine these PoPs at this
time. Adding to this uncertainty, some deterministic guidance 
depicts MCS activity diving southeast out of the Midwest during 
the day, following the periphery of the ridge. Thus, although rain
appears likely at some point on Saturday, the details remain 
unclear at this time. For now, the NBM keeps PoPs generally low, 
maximized in the 20-30% range, to account for this. Meanwhile, 
northerly postfrontal winds will keep highs in the upper 80s on 
Saturday afternoon, with low 90s near the KY/TN line. 

Rain chances look lower from Sunday onward as the upper level 
ridge begins to expand to the east. With surface high pressure 
building to the northeast of the forecast area, northeasterly 
winds will keep Sundays temperatures cooler than at the start of 
the period (but still quite warm). Dewpoints look to be modestly 
lower as well (in the 60s rather than the 70s), and this dry 
pattern will continue through the end of the period. Even so, 
Labor Day looks to be quite warm, with above average temperatures 
in the upper 80s expected across the area. Other than this the 
weather will be quite pleasant and sunny, with the exception of an
isolated diurnally driven thunderstorm in far southeastern 
Kentucky.
